head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Subarray sum = difference of two prefix sums
Highest and lowest prefix sum seen, both starting at 0 for the empty prefix
The largest difference between any two prefix sums is the largest absolute subarray sum, whichever comes first

blocks.h: Why max prefix minus min prefix?
p: Any subarray sum is prefix[j] − prefix[i]. The largest absolute value of such a difference is max(prefix) − min(prefix), because we can pick the pair (min, max) in either order and the absolute value ignores the sign.

1749.takeaway: Maximum |subarray sum| = (max prefix sum) − (min prefix sum), both including the empty prefix 0.

head: Code
What it does

rows: The distinct frequencies; if all frequencies are equal, the set has exactly one element
True when every character appears the same number of times

blocks.h: Why a set of the counts?
p: We don't care which characters have which count, only whether all counts are identical. Collapsing the counts into a set removes duplicates, so one remaining element means they all agree.

1941.takeaway: Count characters, then check that the set of counts has exactly one value.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Union-Find (disjoint set): every node starts as its own root
Walks to the root while shortening paths (`p[x] = p[p[x]]`)
Merges the components of a and b

p: Triangle `0–1–2–0`, source 0, destination 2:
bullets: find(0) = 2, find(2) = 2: equal, so a path exists.

blocks.h: Why Union-Find and not BFS (Breadth-First Search)?
p: Both are O(n + E). Union-Find avoids building adjacency lists and recursion, and is handy when the question is only 'connected or not'. BFS/DFS is better if the actual path were needed.

1971.takeaway: Union all edges; the answer is whether source and destination share a root.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Merge: double the first, zero the second (done left to right, in place, as the statement requires)
[x for x in nums if x]
Keeps the non-zero values in order

blocks.h: Why do the merges happen before the shift?
p: The statement applies the operations in index order on the original positions, and zeros inserted by a merge may sit between equal numbers (e.g. `2, 2, 2`: after merging the first two, the third no longer matches a neighbour). Shifting zeros only after all operations avoids changing which pairs are adjacent.

2460.takeaway: Apply merges left to right in place, then move zeros to the end by filtering and padding.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: End of the previous chosen palindrome; the next one must start at or after it (non-overlapping)
Only lengths k and k + 1 need checking: any longer palindrome (length ≥ k) contains a palindrome of length k or k+1 at its centre
A candidate ending at i must start after `last`
Palindrome check by comparing with the reversed string
Take the earliest-ending palindrome: leaves the most room for later ones

p: `s = "abaccdbbd"`, `k = 3`:

blocks.h: Why is taking the earliest-ending palindrome optimal?
p: This is interval scheduling: among non-overlapping intervals, always finishing as early as possible leaves the most room. Shorter palindromes are enough because a longer palindrome of length ≥ k+2 contains a palindrome of length k or k+1 within it that ends earlier or at the same place.

bullets: Time: O(n · k) (each check is O(k)).

2472.takeaway: Greedy interval scheduling: scan end positions, check palindromes of length k and k+1, take the first that starts after the last chosen end.

Snapshot of the 2-digit subsequence counts for the prefix BEFORE position i
Same from the right: counts of 'ab' subsequences in the suffix after i
A length-5 palindrome is a b ? b a: the pair 'ab' on the left of the middle i and 'ba' on the right
The middle needs two positions on each side

p: `s = "103301"`: middle positions with non-zero contributions (pre count × suf count):

blocks.h: Why fix the middle and multiply?
p: A palindrome subsequence of length 5 is ab?ba. Once the middle position i is fixed, the left pair and the right pair are chosen independently from the prefix and suffix, so their counts multiply. Pre-computed tables make each (i, pair) an O(1) lookup.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Flood fill labels each node with its connected component
BFS (Breadth-First Search) from every node s
Computes layer numbers (distance) from s; the groups are the layers: nodes at distance d go in group d + 1
An edge joining two nodes in the same layer means the component is not bipartite (it has an odd cycle), so valid groups can't exist
Number of layers when starting from s
For each component, the best start gives the most groups
Components are independent, so their group counts add

p: Edges `[[1,2],[1,4],[1,5],[2,6],[2,3],[4,6]]` (one component of 6 nodes). Layers when starting from each node s:
bullets: The best start gives 4 groups: answer 4. A triangle `1–2–3–1` returns -1, because two nodes in the same layer are adjacent.

p: The number of layers depends on where BFS starts. The longest possible layering of a component is achieved from some node (an endpoint of its longest shortest-path), and trying every node finds it. Start nodes whose layering has an intra-layer edge reveal an odd cycle.

2493.takeaway: Connected components, then BFS from every node: layer count is the group count; an edge inside a layer means -1.

Keeps the result non-negative (Python's % already does)

p: `n = 3`: each of the 3 monkeys moves clockwise or counter-clockwise, 2³ = 8 combinations:

Two monkeys collide when they use the same edge in opposite directions or end on the same vertex. The only way for none to collide is for all to move the same way around the polygon, giving exactly 2 outcomes; everything else has at least one collision.

2550.takeaway: Total 2^n moves minus the 2 collision-free ones (all clockwise or all counter-clockwise).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Latest index in s where the suffix t[j:] can start as a subsequence (n + 1 if impossible)
Smallest index such that t[k:] still fits after the matched prefix t[:p]
How much of t's prefix has been matched greedily from the left
Characters t[p:k] are the ones removed: the score is the length of the removed segment (right − left + 1)
The suffix start must lie strictly after the prefix match at i; otherwise shorten the kept suffix

p: `s = "abacaba"`, `t = "bzaa"`: suffix positions `suf = [8, 8, 4, 6, 7]` (index in s where t[j:] can start from the right):
bullets: Removing just `z` leaves `baa`, which is a subsequence of `abacaba`, so the minimum score is 1.

p: Removing t[left..right] keeps a prefix t[:left] and a suffix t[right+1:] that must both be subsequences of s, in order, without overlapping. Greedy left matching gives each prefix its earliest end; greedy right matching gives each suffix its latest start; two pointers choose the smallest removal.

2565.takeaway: Match a prefix of t greedily from the left and a suffix from the right; the removed middle segment is the score.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The two lowest bits are `11`: adding 1 carries and clears a run of 1s (better than subtracting)
Each is one operation (add or subtract a power of two): fixing the lowest set bit is the greedy choice
Even number: shifting right just moves on to the next bit, at no cost

blocks.h: Why add when the low bits are 11?
p: A run of ones such as `0111` costs 3 operations by subtracting each power but only 2 by adding the lowest (`+1` turns it into `1000`, then `-8`). So when two ones are adjacent, add 1; for an isolated one, subtract it. (A lone `…011` pattern with value 3 is the standard exception: 3 costs 2 either way.)

2571.takeaway: Greedy on the low bits: a trailing 11 means add 1, an isolated 1 means subtract it, an even value just shifts.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-heap: always expand the cell reachable earliest
You must move every second; if both first steps are locked at time 1 you are stuck and can't wait at the start
Enter the neighbour at the earliest time it is open
You cannot stand still, but you can bounce back and forth between two cells, wasting time in steps of 2; so the extra waiting time must be even

p: The grid from the problem (cells expanded in order of earliest arrival time):

If a cell opens later than t + 1, you must kill time by stepping back and forth, which takes 2 steps per loop. You can therefore arrive at time (t + 1) + 2k, never at an odd offset. Rounding the wait up to an even number gives the true earliest arrival.

2577.takeaway: Dijkstra where entering a cell waits until it opens, with the wait rounded to an even number (you can only bounce back and forth).
